blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we begin high above the Earth, with a space telescope that found something it never looked for.
Then we visit an ancient forest, where a tiny lizard left its tail behind — on purpose!
Ready?
Let's go!
Meet Euclid, a space telescope from Europe.
Its job is to take slow, steady photos of faraway galaxies, and to study two invisible mysteries: dark matter and dark energy.
Euclid is like a careful photographer of the deep sky.
It was never built to chase fast little comets.
Then, out of the blue, a streak appeared!
In photos of the same patch of sky, a small smudge had moved.
A young scientist in Finland, Mikko Pöntinen, had written clever software to catch moving objects — and it waved a little flag.
In five sets of photos, the smudge had jumped to a new spot each time, circled by a fuzzy cloud of dust and gas.
No flying saucer from a cartoon — a comet, a giant snowball of ice and rock.
But was it really new?
Scientists checked every catalogue of comets and asteroids to determine the truth — no match.
The world centre for small space objects confirmed it: brand new — and it now carries the telescope's name.
It sits about one point three billion kilometres away, between the paths of Jupiter and Saturn, and one trip around the Sun takes thousands of years.
A bonus guest, out of the blue!
Now let's fly back to an ancient forest in Myanmar, where dinosaurs walked.
Sticky resin flowed down a tree, and one golden drop of it trapped something amazing: the tail of a small lizard — skin, muscle and tiny bones, still there ninety-nine million years later.
Today that drop is hard amber, and the tail waits inside it like a message in a bottle.
But why was there only a tail?
Because the lizard dropped it — on purpose!
Many lizards still do this.
When a hungry predator grabs the tail, the tail breaks away and keeps wiggling, distracting the hunter with a snack it can hardly digest — while the lizard dashes free!
Scientists scanned the amber with special X-rays and found a neat muscle pattern inside — the same one modern lizards use to let go.
Direct proof that the trick is ancient!
Still, escape is a compromise.
Without a tail, a lizard climbs and balances more slowly, and a new one takes long to grow.
But the maths was simple: lose a tail, keep a life!
Its tail stayed in the golden amber, waiting to tell its story.
Here's today's idiom: "out of the blue." If something happens out of the blue, it happens suddenly, with no warning at all — like a comet appearing in a quiet photo!
Here's an example: "We were walking home when, out of the blue, it began to rain." Can you remember a surprise from out of the blue?
Let's think about today's stories.
A telescope found a new comet by accident, and a tail in amber proved lizards have used the same escape trick for millions of years.
Now, two questions for you.
First: what surprise would you love to find hiding in an old photo?
Second: the lizard gave up its tail and saved its life — when is giving something up the smart thing to do?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Keep your eyes open — the next big surprise might appear out of the blue!
See you tomorrow morning!
